en.title: Greeting and saying goodbye
en.goal: Greet someone, say goodbye and say thank you in a basic interaction.

lessons.saudacoes: Greeting in the morning and at night

duibuqi-vs-meiguanxi.title: "Duìbuqǐ" or "méi guānxi"?
duibuqi-vs-meiguanxi.body: Duìbuqǐ (对不起) is what you say to apologize. Méi guānxi (没关系) is the reply from the person receiving the apology — "it's okay, no problem." They are the two halves of one exchange, not synonyms: you never use méi guānxi to apologize, or duìbuqǐ to reassure someone.

bu-negation.title: 不 (bù) — the standard negation
bu-negation.body: 不 (bù) is the most common negation in Chinese — it always comes before the verb or adjective you want to negate. Like English "not", it doesn't change its form depending on who is speaking.

zaijian-baibai.title: "再见" often becomes "拜拜" in everyday speech
zaijian-baibai.body: 再见 (zàijiàn) is the standard goodbye and is always correct. In everyday speech, especially among younger people, it's very common to hear 拜拜 (bàibài) — borrowed from English "bye-bye" — instead of 再见, especially on the phone or in messages.

duibuqi-buhaoyisi.title: For small things, "对不起" often becomes "不好意思"
duibuqi-buhaoyisi.body: 对不起 (duìbuqǐ) is the standard way to apologize, but in everyday life it can sound too heavy for small things — bumping into someone, arriving a little late, interrupting. For those situations, it's much more common to hear 不好意思 (bù hǎoyìsi), a lighter apology, a bit like "my bad" or "excuse me."
examples: my bad / excuse me (light apology, small things)

zaoshang-hao-zao.title: "早上好" often becomes just "早" in everyday speech
zaoshang-hao-zao.body: 早上好 (zǎoshang hǎo) is the full, polite way to say "good morning." In everyday life, among people who already know each other — coworkers, neighbors, friends — it's much more common to hear just 早 (zǎo), literally "early." Using the full form with someone close can even sound a bit too formal.

trueFalse.claim: This is what we say when we receive a gift from someone.
trueFalse.whyNote: Correct — 谢谢 (xièxiè) means "thank you," used whenever someone does something for you, including giving you a gift.
